title: Review: IE evidence for sub-shells (period 3 dips); Covalent and dative bonding; Lewis structures; Electronegativity, polarity and intermolecular forces
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD02#t3 term and clue written for the game; AS06#t2 term and clue written for the game; BD04#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD04#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AS06#N.6, BD02#N.2, BD04#N.14, AS06#N.4, BD02#N.11, BD04#N.7a, AS06#N.10, BD02#N.12b, BD04#N.2a, BD04#N.12a, BD04#N.4a, BD04#N.9a. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Octet rule
items.clue: The tendency of atoms to end up with eight outer electrons.

items.label: Sub-shell
items.clue: A division of a main level, such as 3s or 3p, with its own energy.

items.label: Electronegativity
items.clue: The ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair in a covalent bond.

items.label: London forces
items.clue: Electron movement makes a temporary dipole that induces one in a nearby molecule.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energies of phosphorus and sulfur are 1012 kJ mol⁻¹ and 1000 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the lower value for sulfur is correct?

options.text: Sulfur's outer electrons are shielded by more inner electrons than phosphorus's.
Sulfur's electron is removed from a sub-shell of higher energy than phosphorus's.
Sulfur loses an electron from a doubly occupied 3p orbital, where repulsion raises its energy.
Sulfur atoms are larger than phosphorus atoms, so their outer electron is further away.

questions.explanation: P has three unpaired 3p electrons; in S one 3p orbital holds a pair. Repulsion between them means slightly less energy is needed.

questions.stem: What holds the hydrogen atom and the chlorine atom together in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?

options.text: The need of each atom to gain a full outer shell by sharing a pair of electrons
The shared pair of electrons itself, acting as a physical link between the atoms
The electrostatic attraction of both nuclei to a shared pair of electrons
The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions H⁺ and Cl⁻

questions.explanation: The shared pair lies between the H and Cl nuclei and is attracted to both. That attraction is the covalent bond.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃ (Mᵣ 17.0), boils at −33 °C. Phosphine, PH₃ (Mᵣ 34.0), boils at −88 °C. Electronegativity: H 2.2, N 3.0, P 2.2. Why does the lighter molecule boil higher?

options.text: PH₃ molecules have no forces between them, because their P–H bonds are non-polar.
NH₃ has stronger London forces than PH₃, because it is the smaller molecule.
NH₃ molecules hydrogen bond to each other; PH₃ molecules cannot.
Boiling NH₃ breaks its N–H bonds, which are stronger than P–H bonds.

questions.explanation: N is very electronegative, so N–H is δ+ at H, and each N has a lone pair: N–H⋯N hydrogen bonds. P–H bonds are hardly polar (both 2.2), so PH₃ has no hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: After the dip, the rise resumes: silicon's first ionisation energy is 787 kJ mol⁻¹, higher than aluminium's 578 kJ mol⁻¹. Why?

options.text: Silicon's electron is removed from 3s, which is lower in energy than aluminium's 3p.
Silicon's two 3p electrons are paired in one orbital, which holds them more firmly.
Silicon atoms are larger, so there is more space for the nucleus to attract its electrons.
Both electrons come from 3p, but silicon has one more proton and similar shielding.

questions.explanation: Same sub-shell, similar shielding, greater nuclear charge: the attraction is stronger, so more energy is needed.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, reacts with a hydrogen ion, H⁺, to form the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. Which statement about the bonds in NH₄⁺ is correct?

options.text: The bond formed from the lone pair on nitrogen is longer and weaker than the other three N–H bonds
The new bond formed from a pair of electrons supplied by the H⁺ ion to nitrogen
The new bond formed from one electron supplied by nitrogen and one electron supplied by H⁺
All four N–H bonds are identical, although one formed from the lone pair on nitrogen

questions.explanation: The new bond is co-ordinate: both electrons from N. Once formed, all four N–H bonds have the same length and strength.

questions.stem: Liquid methanol, CH₃OH, contains hydrogen bonds. What is a hydrogen bond in methanol?

options.text: An attraction between the H of an O–H group and a lone pair on O in another molecule
The covalent bond between the O atom and the H atom within one methanol molecule
An attraction between the H atoms of one molecule and the H atoms of another
An attraction between an H atom of the CH₃ group and an O atom in a neighbouring molecule

questions.explanation: H bonded to O is δ+, and it is attracted to a lone pair on the O of a neighbour.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energies of beryllium and boron are 900 kJ mol⁻¹ and 801 kJ mol⁻¹. Which explanation of the lower value for boron is correct?

options.text: Boron's electron is removed from a 2p orbital that already holds another electron.
Boron atoms are larger than beryllium atoms, so the outer electron is further away.
Boron's electron is removed from 2p, which is higher in energy than beryllium's 2s.
Boron's nuclear charge is shared among more electrons, so each is held less strongly.

questions.stem: Carbon monoxide, CO, has 10 outer electrons, the same as N₂. Like N₂, it has a triple bond and one lone pair on each atom. Which describes the three shared pairs?

options.text: Three ordinary covalent bonds: C and O each supply three electrons.
Two ordinary covalent bonds, plus one co-ordinate bond from C to O.
Three co-ordinate bonds, all from O to C.
Two ordinary covalent bonds, plus one co-ordinate bond from O to C.

questions.explanation: C shares two electrons and O two: two ordinary pairs. O then donates one lone pair to C: C≡O with an arrow O→C. Each atom keeps one lone pair and has 8.

questions.stem: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, F 4.0, P 2.2. Which bond is the most polar?

options.text: O–H
O–F
C–F
P–H

questions.explanation: 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4, the largest difference, so the pair is pulled most towards F.

questions.stem: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane, C₆H₁₄, does not dissolve in water. Which statement explains this difference?

options.text: Ethanol splits into ions that water surrounds, but hexane does not form ions
Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, but hexane cannot
Hexane is less dense than water, so it floats on the water rather than dissolving
Hexane molecules are too large to fit into the gaps between water molecules

questions.explanation: Ethanol's O–H hydrogen bonds to water, replacing the ones broken. Hexane offers only weak London forces.

questions.stem: Water, H₂O, is a polar molecule with a permanent dipole (electronegativity: H 2.2, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its O–H bonds are polar, and every molecule with polar bonds has a permanent dipole
It is bent, so its two O–H bond dipoles do not point in opposite directions
Its H atoms lie at 90° to each other, as in its dot-and-cross diagram, so the dipoles add
Its oxygen atom has two lone pairs, which are the only source of its permanent dipole

questions.explanation: Each O–H is δ− at O. At about 104.5° the two dipoles add to a resultant.

questions.stem: Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃ (Mᵣ 44.11), ethanal, CH₃CHO (Mᵣ 44.06), and ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH (Mᵣ 46.08), have comparable molar masses. Which lists them in order of increasing boiling point?

options.text: propane < ethanal < ethanol
propane < ethanol < ethanal
ethanal < propane < ethanol
ethanal < ethanol < propane

questions.explanation: Similar masses, so the force type decides: London only (−42 °C), dipole–dipole added (20 °C), hydrogen bonds (78 °C).
